actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: The species Anemonia viridis (= A. sulcata) has an Atlanto-Mediterranean distribution (Chintiroglou et al. 1997). It is widespread over the entire Mediterranean basin, being one of the most common anthozoans (Carpine 1987). It has been reported from many parts of the western and the central Mediterranean, from the Adriatic, North Africa, the Levantine basin (Egypt, Israel, Chypre) and the Aegean Sea (Gili 1981; Chintiroglou 1987; Chintiroglou et al. 1997; Vafidis et al. 1997; Ocaña et al. 2000; Kruzic 2002, 2007; Badalamenti et al., 2011; Boumediene and Djillali, 2014; Horwitz et al., 2014; Jimenez, per. comm. 2015). It is common in the Dardanelles (Zdenek et al. 2013, B. Ozalp pers. obs. 2014).
documentation.population:
It is generally considered as the most common sea anemone species in the sublittoral zone. 

The population density and trends of Anemonia viridis in the Mediterranean have been scarcely investigated. Some data exist from the north Aegean Sea reporting 6 to 25 individuals /m2 for Chalkidiki peninsula (Glaropoulos et al. 2006). In high-density sites the pattern of dispersion has been investigated by applying Morisita’s index, and found to be aggregated (Margaritis et al. 2006). In one location of Thermaikos Gulf a very dense A. viridis population has been seasonally studied; mean density ranged from 472 individuals/m2, in autumn, to 948 individuals/m2, in summer, with an overall mean at 691 individuals/m2 (Chintiroglou and Koukouras 1992). Relevant data from several (29 stations) stations along the coastline of Thermaikos Gulf reported density differences with respect to the habitat type sampled; thus, in shallow infralittoral pebbles (1m depth) the mean density of A. viridis was 24.5 individuals/m2); in coarse sands interspersed with rather sparse Posidonia meadows (2m depth) population density reached 59 individuals/m2, and in photophilic algae communities interspersed on Zostera rhizomes, sands and pebbles (2m depth) a density of of 132 individuals /m2 was reported (Chintiroglou 1996).

More recent data recorded from a 3-year survey in Thermaikos Gulf suggested a possible declining population as density decreased from 130 individuals/m2 in 2001 to 100 individuals/m2 in 2002 and to 51 individuals/m2 in 2003 (Chintiroglou et al. 2003). However a recent survey in the same area (May 2014) reported a well –developed A. viridis carpet in the shallow (2 m depth) sublittoral zone of the same area (NE coast of Thessaloniki Bay, Thermaikos Gulf (Chintiroglou and Antoniadou, unpublished data). Aggregated populations under favorable conditions have been reported for the species, as well as a depth segregated pattern in size and density (Chintiroglou 1998).

Overall trends in the Mediterranean are seem to be stable; quantitative data from the south coast of Spain support stability despite relatively high exploitation (Terron-Sigler pers. comm. 2014). The species is generally considered as very common and able to form very dense populations under appropriate environmental conditions.
documentation.habitats: The species Anemonia viridis lives in various habitat types; in pools, attached to rocks or various algae, on seagrass meadows and on soft substrata, in sandy sediment with pebbles and gravels (Chintiroglou 1987), from the lower mid littoral to the sub littoral zone down to 25 m depth. A. viridis reproduces both sexually and asexually (Chintiroglou 1996).
documentation.threats: Main threats for the species are harvesting for consumption in Spain, the south coast of Italy and Sardinia; however official data are absent from most locations. Additional impacts from coastal development are suspected.
documentation.measures: There are no active conservation measures for the species. The species is present in marine protected areas (e.g., Telascica Nature Park; Mljet, National Marine Park of Northerns Sporades, Al-Hoceima National Park).
documentation.use_trade: Anemonia viridis is an edible species, being typically consumed in Italy, Greece and South Spain (Marino 1958, Carpine 1987). It is not frequently present in Mediterranean markets, although it can be found in many seafood restaurants over the Greek territory, especially in Pagasitikos Gulf and in Cadiz region (Spain).
documentation.rationale: The species has been recorded from the entire Mediterranean and it seems to be very common, locally forming very dense aggregations; there is limited information on population density and trends. This species is harvested for consumption in certain localities, but this does not appear to be negatively impacting the population at present. Given the wide distribution and existence of dense aggregations, this species is assessed as Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: This species is known as A. sulcata in the Mediterranean and as A. viridis in the Atlantic, but it is one species.
